0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what R.C. Sproul called “the most majestic letter Paul ever penned” — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens with one of the most breathtaking passages in all of Scripture — a single unbroken sentence in the Greek, 202 words long, a cascade of praise that pours out of him like a river that has broken its banks. Before a single command is given, before a single duty is laid upon the Ephesians, Paul gives them six magnificent verses of pure gift: what God has done, is doing, and will do for His people in Christ. The grammar of grace always works this way — indicative before imperative, blessing before obligation, the gift before the task. You cannot rightly obey what you have not first received.

The structure of the passage is trinitarian and it is deliberate. The Father chooses and adopts (vv.3–6); the Son redeems and reconciles (vv.7–12); the Spirit seals and guarantees (vv.13–14). Every Person of the Godhead is active in our salvation. Every blessing flows from the coordinated purpose of the triune God. And the scope is cosmic — from before the foundation of the world, when we were chosen in Christ before time began, to the fullness of time, when all things in heaven and on earth will be united in Him. We are not an afterthought in God's plan. We are its centrepiece, its showcase, the display case for the riches of His grace in the ages to come.

Count the phrase "in Christ" or "in him." It appears eleven times in twelve verses. Every single blessing — election, adoption, redemption, forgiveness, inheritance, sealing — is located not in ourselves, not in our performance, not even in our faith as such, but in Christ. We have these things because we are in Him. This is the most important prepositional phrase in the Christian life. To be in Christ is to have everything. To be outside of Christ is to have nothing, however religious, however moral, however sincere one might be. The entire letter of Ephesians is an unpacking of what it means to be in Christ — and it begins here, with a doxology so full and so free it can barely be contained in sentences.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of His will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of His grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apostolos means “sent one” — the word used for an official ambassador carrying the full authority of the one who dispatched him. The qualifier “by the will of God” is not incidental: Paul’s authority to declare the mystery of God’s purposes in chapters 2–3 rests entirely on this commission. He did not volunteer; he was made.

“Saints” (hagioi) — set-apart ones, holy ones. Not a title earned by moral achievement but a status conferred by belonging to God. In Paul’s vocabulary every believer is a saint. The word is used nine times in Ephesians; it is the community’s foundational identity before any conduct is described.

Some manuscripts omit “in Ephesus,” suggesting the letter may have circulated as a general epistle to the churches of the region. This does not diminish its authority; it extends its reach.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The standard Pauline greeting, but never merely formulaic. Charis (grace) transforms the ordinary Greek greeting chairein into a theological declaration: the entire gift of God’s undeserved favour. Eirene (peace) carries the Hebrew shalom: not the absence of conflict but the positive flourishing of a life rightly ordered to God.

The double source — “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” — places Father and Son on the same grammatical and theological level as the single origin of both gifts. Casual Trinitarian theology, stated before the letter has even begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three uses of the blessing root (eulogeo / eulogia) in one verse: God is to be blessed (praised) because he has blessed (given) us. The blessings are “spiritual” — not meaning immaterial, but coming from and consisting in the Holy Spirit. “Every” spiritual blessing: not some, not the ones we have earned, but the entire treasury. The word “in Christ” will govern the entire doxology: every blessing is located in him, accessible only through union with him.

“Heavenly places” (epouraniois) is a phrase unique to Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). It describes the realm of spiritual reality where the decisive events occur and from which the decisive blessings flow. The Christian’s life is simultaneously earthly and heavenly — the blessings are already fully given in the heavenly realm even while they are being worked out on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Election. Before creation existed, before time began, before any human merit was possible or conceivable, God chose his people in Christ. The basis is entirely within God — no human quality, no foreseen faith, no anticipated response provided the grounds.

The purpose of election is stated immediately: “that we should be holy and blameless before him.” Election is not a doctrine for theological argument; it is a doctrine for worship and moral transformation. The one who knows he was chosen before the world began has the deepest possible motivation for the holiness that was the purpose of that choosing. Election precedes holiness; it does not replace it.

What does “holy” mean here? The Greek word is hagios — set apart, consecrated, belonging entirely to God. In the Old Testament, the vessels of the Temple were “holy” not because they were morally flawless but because they were reserved exclusively for God’s use. When Paul says God chose us to be hagios, he means: set apart from the world’s ownership and set apart for God’s. The primary meaning is relational and positional before it is behavioural: we belong to him. That belonging then reshapes everything — how we think, what we love, how we treat others, what we pursue. Holiness is not the entry requirement; it is the destination God is moving his people toward. 1 Peter 1:15–16: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct.”

What does “blameless” mean here? The Greek is amōmos — without blemish, without spot. It is the word used in the Septuagint for a sacrificial animal that is fit for offering: no defect, no disqualification. It carries a forensic dimension — standing before God without charge, nothing held against us — as well as a moral dimension: a life that does not give the accuser legitimate grounds. “Before him” is the crucial phrase: blameless in God’s sight, not in our own estimation or other people’s assessment.

Does Paul mean moral perfection? No — and this is essential to understand, because many believers read these words and feel condemned rather than called. Paul is speaking of two things at once, and both matter:

  • Present standing by imputation. The believer in Christ is already declared holy and blameless before God — not because of their own record but because they are clothed in Christ’s righteousness. This is the “in him” of the verse: chosen in Christ, accepted in Christ, presented holy and blameless in Christ. Col. 1:22: “he has now reconciled [you] in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him.” This standing is the unshakeable foundation. The believer who is still struggling with sin is no less holy and blameless before God because the holiness and blamelessness being counted is Christ’s.
  • Future completion by transformation. At the same time, Paul looks forward to what God is progressively accomplishing in his people, and what will be fully realised at the last day. Phil. 1:10: “so that you may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ.” Jude 24: “now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy.” The goal of election is a people fully conformed to the image of Christ — which the New Testament consistently says is not yet fully achieved but is certain to be completed. 1 John 3:2: “we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

These two dimensions belong together. The standing gives the struggling Christian their footing: “God sees me in Christ; I am not disqualified.” The trajectory gives them their direction: “this is where God is taking me; I am not finished yet.” The person who only has the standing becomes complacent; the person who only has the trajectory becomes despairing. Paul gives both — chosen to be holy and blameless, which means God both declares it and intends to complete it.

Practical implication. A believer who has sinned badly this week does not stand before God with a diminished holiness, because their holiness is not measured by this week. They stand before God in the righteousness of Christ, which is constant and sufficient. That is not a licence to continue sinning (Rom. 6:1–2); it is the mercy that makes genuine repentance possible — you can return to God without first having made yourself presentable, because Christ has already made you so. cf. Col. 1:22; Phil. 1:10; Jude 24; 1 John 3:2; Rom. 8:29–30; 2 Tim. 1:9.

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In love” almost certainly modifies predestination rather than what precedes: it was in love that he predestined. Predestination is not cold decree but the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children. The warmth of the word “adoption” confirms it.

“Adoption” (huiothesia) is a legal term for the full conferral of sonship on someone not born to it. Roman adoption was irrevocable and conferred complete inheritance rights. The adopted son had all the standing of a biological heir — the past could not reclaim him. “According to the purpose of his will” — the ground is entirely within God. This is not a harsh doctrine; it is the guarantee of its permanence.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of three “to the praise of his glory” refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), marking the three Trinitarian movements of the doxology. Every section ends at the same destination: God praised. Salvation has a design beyond the saved.

“The Beloved” — a title for Christ that echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism (“This is my beloved Son”) and the transfiguration. The blessings come to us because we are in the one who is supremely loved. We receive what belongs to him because we are in him.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Redemption” (apolutrosis) is the language of the slave market and the exodus: the payment of a price to secure release. The price is specific: his blood. Not his teaching, not his example, not his moral influence — his blood. Forgiveness is the content of what redemption achieves: the actual cancellation of actual sins.

“According to the riches of his grace” — not the minimum, not the merely adequate, but proportioned to the wealth of God’s own grace. This is a lavish transaction, not a careful one. (cf. Col. 1:14; 1 Pet. 1:18–19)

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Lavished” — poured out abundantly, overflowing. God did not give grace carefully, measuring out precisely what was sufficient. He poured. The grace is not sentimental, however: it was given “in all wisdom and insight” — with full knowledge of what we are and what we need. The lavishness and the wisdom belong together: it is not reckless giving but intelligent abundance.

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “mystery” (mystērion) is not a puzzle but a previously hidden plan now disclosed. What had been concealed across the ages — how God would deal with sin, unite divided humanity, and bring all creation under one head — has now been unveiled in Christ. Paul uses “mystery” seven times in Ephesians alone; the word always carries this sense: not unknowable, but once-hidden-now-revealed. cf. Rom. 16:25–26: “the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed.”

God’s ultimate purpose is stated with one magnificent Greek word: anakephalāiosis — re-heading, summing up, gathering under one head. The prefix ana carries the idea of restoration to an original order; kephalē is head. What was once unified under God’s good order was shattered by the fall: God and humanity estranged, humans estranged from one another, creation groaning under the curse, spiritual powers in rebellion. God’s plan, purposed before creation (v.4), is the reunification of everything — “things in heaven and things on earth” — under the one true head, Jesus Christ.

What does it mean to “unite all things in Christ”? The fall did not merely damage individual human souls — it fractured the entire order of reality. Romans 8:20–22 says the whole creation was subjected to futility and has been groaning. The spiritual realm was thrown into disorder by angelic rebellion. Human society became a theatre of war, exploitation, and injustice. Death entered. Decay entered. Every dimension of existence lost its proper orientation toward God.

To unite all things in Christ means God is not simply rescuing souls out of a ruined world and abandoning the rest. He is restoring everything to its right relationship with its true head. Think of what happens to a body when the head is rightly connected and functioning: every limb, every organ, every system finds its proper role and operates as it was designed. Christ as head of all things means: everything re-ordered, re-purposed, restored to the glory it was made to display. “He is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Col. 1:17) — what holds together now by his sustaining power will one day be fully, visibly, gloriously ordered under him. Col. 1:19–20: “through him to reconcile to himself all things… making peace by the blood of his cross.”

Why “things” and not “people”? This is a fair and important question. The Greek is ta panta — all things, the totality of what exists, not merely persons. Paul deliberately uses the impersonal neuter plural. Why?

  • Because the fall affected more than people. Sin dislocated the entire created order — not only human hearts but nature (Gen. 3:17–18; Rom. 8:20), structures of power, spiritual realities, and the fabric of time and space itself. God’s redemption is correspondingly comprehensive. It would be too small a salvation if it only rescued individuals while leaving the cosmos broken.
  • Because spiritual powers are included. Elsewhere in Ephesians Paul writes of “rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” (3:10; 6:12) — angelic and demonic powers whose rebellion fractured the spiritual order. Col. 2:15 says Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.” Their defeat and final subjection is part of the uniting of all things. 1 Cor. 15:24–28 describes Christ delivering the kingdom to the Father after destroying every rule, authority, and power. The “things in heaven” are not the redeemed in glory — they are the spiritual realm itself, brought into rightful subjection under Christ’s headship.
  • Because the new creation is physical. Paul does not envision God discarding the material world and retreating to a purely spiritual realm. The resurrection of Christ’s body is the prototype: matter redeemed, transformed, glorified — not abandoned. Rev. 21:1–5 pictures a new heaven and new earth, not the dissolution of earth into heaven. “Things on earth” will be renewed, not erased.

Things in heaven and things on earth. Together these two phrases cover the totality of existence — the idiom of comprehensiveness that Hebrew thinking expressed as “heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Nothing is outside the scope of what Christ will reclaim. There is no zone of creation that falls outside his redemptive purpose — no corner of the cosmos that will remain broken, disordered, or under the dominion of the enemy when the plan reaches its fullness.

The “fullness of time” (plērōma tōn kairōn) speaks of God’s sovereign timing: history is not random but directed, moving toward a divinely appointed moment of completion. Gal. 4:4–5: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.” The incarnation was the hinge; the consummation will be the goal. Rev. 21:5: “Behold, I am making all things new.” 1 Cor. 15:27–28: “he has put all things under his feet… that God may be all in all.”

For the believer, this vision is both humbling and exhilarating. You are not living in a random universe drifting toward chaos. You are living inside a plan conceived before creation, executed at the cross, and moving inexorably toward the moment when every fractured thing — every broken relationship, every groaning creature, every rebellious power — is gathered, re-ordered, and summed up under the one who holds all things together. cf. Col. 1:17–20; Col. 2:15; Rom. 8:19–22; Gal. 4:4–5; 1 Cor. 15:24–28; Rev. 21:1–5.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In him we have obtained an inheritance.” Two enormous truths are packed into this half-verse. Before unpacking the inheritance, Paul roots it in the words that have appeared again and again in this opening doxology: in him.

“In him” — the most important two words in Ephesians. Paul has already used this phrase or its equivalent nine times in verses 3–13 alone. It is not a throwaway preposition. It describes the believer’s entire location before God: not standing in their own name, not presenting their own record, not approaching on the basis of their own history — but in Christ, clothed in him, hidden in him, identified with him, accepted because he is accepted.

Think of what this means. Every blessing in verse 3 comes in him. Election before the foundation of the world is in him (v.4). Adoption is in him (v.5). Redemption and forgiveness are in him (v.7). The mystery of God’s purposes is disclosed in him (v.9). And now the inheritance is obtained in him.

The believer has no standing apart from Christ — and needs none, because in Christ they have the standing of the Son himself. When God looks at the believer, he sees them in his beloved Son. This is not a legal fiction; it is the most real thing about them. Col. 3:3: “your life is hidden with Christ in God.” 2 Cor. 5:21: “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” John 17:23: “I in them and you in me… that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.” The Father loves the believer with the same love with which he loves the Son — because the believer is found in the Son. Let that settle for a moment.

The inheritance — what is meant here? The Greek word is eklērōthēmen — literally “we were allotted a portion,” the verb used for assigning lots, as land was distributed to the tribes of Israel by lot (Josh. 14:1–2). The inheritance Paul has in mind operates on two levels:

  • God as our inheritance. In the Old Testament, the Levites received no land allotment in Canaan because the Lord himself was their inheritance (Num. 18:20; Ps. 16:5–6). This is the deepest layer of meaning: to be in Christ is to be given God himself — his presence, his love, his glory — as the portion of our souls. The inheritance is not primarily a list of blessings; it is the Giver. Ps. 73:25–26: “whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you… God is… my portion forever.”
  • The eschatological inheritance. Verse 14 will call the Spirit the “guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it.” The inheritance has been granted but not yet fully received — it awaits the final day. This is the language of a will that has been signed and sealed: the heir is certain of what is coming, even though they have not yet taken possession. Peter calls it “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet. 1:4). Paul elsewhere describes it as sharing in the glory of Christ: “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). The full weight of what Christ possesses as the eternal Son — glory, honour, dominion, the new creation — is what the believer inherits in him.

“Who works all things according to the counsel of his will.” One of the strongest statements of divine sovereignty in the New Testament. Not some things. Not most things. All things. The counsel (boulē) is God’s own deliberate plan — not his reaction to human choices but his eternal, unhurried purpose. This is not uncomfortable; it is the ground of confidence that the inheritance will be delivered. The God who works all things according to his will is the God who has promised you the inheritance. It cannot miscarry.

“We who were the first to hope in Christ” likely refers to Jewish believers — those who had the long preparation of the Old Testament promises and were the first to recognise their fulfilment in Jesus — anticipating the Gentile inclusion announced in v.13. The full picture requires both. cf. Col. 3:3; 2 Cor. 5:21; John 17:23; Rom. 8:17; 1 Pet. 1:4; Ps. 16:5–6; Ps. 73:25–26; Num. 18:20.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You also” — now the Gentiles. The same election, the same redemption, the same sealing. The Spirit is the seal: in antiquity a seal conveyed ownership, authenticity, and security. God has stamped his ownership on every believer. The Spirit cannot be revoked; the ownership stands.

The Spirit is also the arrabōn — the guarantee, the down payment, the first instalment of the full inheritance still to come. What the Spirit gives now is not the whole but the taste, the proof, the pledge of everything that is coming. The “until” is eschatological: the Spirit holds the believer sealed until the day the full possession is received. (cf. Rom. 8:16; 2 Cor. 1:22)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul prays. The man who has just outlined the most concentrated doctrinal statement in the New Testament now falls on his knees for the people he loves. And his prayer is not for comfort, not for prosperity, not even for their safety — it is for illumination. He prays that they would know. Not know more information about God — they have just received an overwhelming cascade of theological truth. But know it experientially, vitally, in the way that transforms the soul rather than merely informing the mind. There is a vast difference between possessing a treasure and being fully aware of what you possess. Paul prays to close that gap.

Three things he asks for illumination about, each one more staggering than the last. First: the hope of their calling — the glorious future that God has promised and secured for those who are in Christ. Second: the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints — the almost incomprehensible truth that God Himself regards His people as His inheritance, His treasure, His glory. Third: the immeasurable greatness of His power toward those who believe. And to give the Ephesians a sense of how great that power is, Paul reaches for the most powerful event in history as his measure: the resurrection of Jesus from the dead and His exaltation to the right hand of the Father, far above every name and authority and power in the universe. That power — the power that raised the dead and shattered the dominion of death — is at work in you.

The prayer closes with a vision of Christ as head over all things for the church, which is His body, the fullness of the One who fills all in all. The church is not a voluntary association of like-minded believers. It is the body of the cosmic Lord, the community through which the exalted Christ exercises His reign in the world. To be part of the church is to be part of the most significant institution in the universe — the community of the risen King.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this: they typically spent as much time in prayer before Bible reading as in the reading itself, asking God to grant illumination. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of Him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary: “For this reason” connects back to the entire doxology: because of all that God has done in Christ, Paul prays. Thanksgiving precedes petition — the order is deliberate. The prayer is grounded in what God has already accomplished, not driven by what is still lacking. It is a prayer of grateful sufficiency reaching for greater knowledge, not anxious insufficiency reaching for more resources.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The Father of glory” — a title that gathers everything from the doxology: the God whose very nature is glory, whose purposes produce glory, who acts for the praise of his glory. Every word of the address before the petition is itself worship.

The “Spirit of wisdom and revelation” is not a second giving of the Spirit (already received, v. 13) but the Spirit in his function as illuminator — opening up what is already true about God to the eyes of the heart. Natural intelligence cannot see what Paul is asking God to show. The knowledge of God requires a supernatural gift of perception.

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Eyes of the heart” — in biblical anthropology the heart is not primarily the emotions but the centre of the person, the seat of understanding and will. The heart needs its own eyes: organs of perception that natural intelligence cannot provide. This is why Paul prays rather than simply argues: he knows that what he is asking them to see requires more than information.

“His glorious inheritance in the saints” — notice the direction. Not our inheritance in God (which is also true) but God’s inheritance in us. We are his treasure. The God who owns the universe counts his people as his inheritance. This is not a small thought.

verseByVerse.quote: And what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stacks four Greek words for power in these verses: dunamis (power), energeia (working/energy), kratos (strength/dominion), ischus (force). He is reaching for the limits of the language. No single word is sufficient; he uses all four at once.

The power available to believers is not a metaphor or a pious encouragement — it is specifically identified as the same power that raised a corpse to life and seated it at the right hand of all authority. Resurrection power is the operative power in the Christian life. If you want to know the scale of what God is willing to exert on behalf of those who believe, look at the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary: The ascended Christ is above every hierarchy in the cosmos — angelic, demonic, political, spiritual. “Every name that is named” is a sweep of the entire created order: whatever you can name, Christ is above it. This is not measured language. It is the most comprehensive claim of cosmic lordship in the New Testament, and it is the foundation on which everything in chapters 4–6 rests.

verseByVerse.quote: He put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Gave him as head over all things to the church” — the cosmic headship of Christ over all creation is given as a gift to the church. The one who rules everything rules it on behalf of his people. That is not a small thing to know when the world feels out of control.

“The fullness of him who fills all in all” (to pleroma tou ta panta en pasin pleroumenou) — the infinite Christ, who fills the cosmos, considers the church to be his fullness, his expression in the world. The church is not a religious organisation under Christ’s endorsement. It is the body through which the head who fills all things makes himself visible on earth. (cf. Col. 1:18; 2:10)

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the gospel in its most concentrated and most searching form, and it opens with a diagnosis so radical it takes the breath away. We were dead. Not sick, not wounded, not spiritually impaired — dead. The Greek word is nekros, the same word used for a corpse. Paul is not being poetic; he is being precise. Before God's intervention, the human being in their natural state is spiritually lifeless — incapable of generating their own salvation, incapable of seeking God, incapable even of responding to God without God's prior action. The standard is not low; it is absolute. Dead people do not cooperate with their resurrection. They receive it.

And then — with two words that are among the most glorious in all of Scripture — the diagnosis is shattered by a declaration: But God. Rich in mercy. Because of His great love with which He loved us. Even when we were dead in our trespasses. God acted. He made us alive together with Christ. He raised us up with Him. He seated us with Him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Three movements of sovereign grace, each one more astonishing than the last — and the purpose of all of it: "so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus." We are not saved merely for our own benefit. We are saved to be the eternal showcase of grace — the exhibit that the universe will study for ages to come, marvelling at the kindness of a God who raised the spiritually dead and made them heirs of glory.

The passage closes with one of the clearest articulations of the gospel anywhere in the Bible: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (vv.8–9). And then the stunning turn of v.10: we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works which God prepared beforehand. Salvation is not by works — but it is absolutely for works. Grace is not the enemy of effort; it is the only soil in which genuine, God-honouring effort can grow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the body and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; He acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. Calvin's comment on v.5 is unforgettable: "If we are to seek the cause of our salvation, we shall find it not in ourselves but in God alone." The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself His gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Dead” (nekrous) — not metaphorically weakened but genuinely dead to God, incapable of spiritual response or initiative toward him. Trespasses (paraptomata) are deliberate steppings-across; sins (hamartia) is missing the mark — together they cover the full range of human failure: the deliberate and the inadvertent, the rebellious and the negligent.

“The course of this world” (aion) — the spirit of the age, the invisible current that carries everyone who is not actively swimming against it. “The prince of the power of the air” — Satan, not as a petty adversary but as the ruling spirit behind the age’s direction. The unregenerate person is simultaneously following the crowd and following a cosmic enemy who is directing it. (cf. Col. 2:13; Rom. 3:23)

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We all” — Paul includes himself and Jewish believers. This is not Gentile pathology; it is the human condition without distinction. “Children of wrath” — not people who occasionally attracted God’s wrath but people whose nature was oriented toward the wrath they deserved.

“By nature” (phusei) — this is the Reformed doctrine of original sin in two words. The fallenness is not an external imposition but constitutive of human nature since the fall. The problem is not primarily what we do but what we are.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But God.” Two words. The pivot of the passage, the pivot of redemptive history, the pivot of every Christian life. Everything before: our death, our slavery, our deserved wrath. Everything after: his mercy, his love, his action.

“Rich in mercy” — not adequate mercy, not sufficient mercy — rich, abundant, overflowing. The love is “great” (pollen) and it acted “even when we were dead” — not when we improved, not when we responded, but when we were dead and incapable of response. Salvation is resurrection, and the dead do not cooperate in their own raising. The initiative is entirely God’s. (cf. Titus 3:5; Col. 2:13)

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three verbs, all beginning with “with” (sun-) in Greek: made alive with, raised with, seated with. What happened to Christ has happened to the believer by virtue of union with him. The believer’s status in the heavenly places is not a future aspiration — it is a present reality. Already seated. The positional truth is complete; the experiential reality is being worked out in time.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of salvation includes cosmic display. In the ages to come, every saved sinner will be an exhibit of the riches of God’s grace. The church is God’s trophy case. This is not a secondary purpose; it is the stated reason behind the rescue. God is glorifying himself through the salvation of those who did not deserve it.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “this is not your own doing” most likely refers to the entire salvation package — grace, faith, the whole event — not just the faith. Faith itself is not a human contribution that triggers God’s grace; faith is the instrument through which grace is received, and the whole transaction is the gift of God.

“So that no one may boast” — the design of grace is the elimination of human pride in the transaction of salvation. This is not a consequence Paul has noticed; it is the intention God had. The glory belongs entirely to the Giver. MacArthur has observed: if even one element of salvation depended on human cooperation, the difference between the saved and the unsaved would ultimately be traceable to something in the human — and Paul will not allow that. (cf. Rom. 3:28; Gal. 2:16)

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Workmanship” (poiema) — the word from which “poem” comes. We are God’s work of art, his craftsmanship. The same God who spoke creation into being has spoken new creation into us.

The good works are not the basis of salvation (vv. 8–9) but its purpose — and they are themselves prepared by God in advance. Grace that excludes boasting does not exclude works; it produces them, lays them out like a track, and then enables the redeemed person to walk in them. The obedience is no less real for being prepared; it is no less the believer’s for being given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If vv.1–10 describe the miracle of individual salvation, vv.11–22 describe its corporate consequence — and the consequence is nothing less than the creation of a new humanity. The most profound social division of the ancient world was the division between Jew and Gentile. It was not merely ethnic; it was religious, covenantal, cultic, and moral. The Jew had the oracles of God, the covenants of promise, the temple, the law, the Messiah. The Gentile was "separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (v.12). The wall between them was literal — the Jerusalem temple had a stone barrier (the soreg) beyond which Gentiles could not pass on pain of death. And spiritually, the distance was infinite.

Christ has abolished it. Not by lowering the standard, not by relativising the covenant, not by pretending the distinction never mattered — but by fulfilling what the distinction pointed to and then, in His own body on the cross, "killing the hostility" (v.16). He made peace. Not peace by negotiation, not peace by compromise, but peace by blood — His own blood, shed for both Jew and Gentile, making one new man in place of two. The dividing wall of hostility has been broken down in Christ. The sign above the gate that once said "Keep Out" has been torn down and replaced with a welcome: "You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (v.13).

The result is a building — a temple. Not the old temple in Jerusalem, with its courts of separation and its stone barrier. A new temple, built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. The church is God's dwelling place by the Spirit. What the Jerusalem temple was in shadow, the church now is in reality: the place where God lives, the community through which He makes Himself known to the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded. The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by His Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make His home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity He created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: You were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five descriptions of Gentile exclusion, each one darker than the last. Separated. Alienated. Strangers. No hope. Without God. The worst of the five is the last: atheos — without God. Not atheists in the modern sense, but people from whom God had withdrawn his covenant presence. Surrounded by gods, they were — in the most precise sense — godless.

Paul begins with “remember” (v. 11). The memory of what we were is not guilt-maintenance; it is gratitude-maintenance. You cannot fully receive grace you have forgotten you needed.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “But now” — the second great pivot of chapter 2 (the first was “but God” in v. 4). Far off / brought near is the language of Isaiah 57:19, which Paul will quote in v. 17. The distance has been closed, and the means is specific: blood. Not dialogue, not mutual understanding, not the passage of time, not a shared commitment to common values — blood.

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He himself is our peace” — not the bringer of peace but peace itself. Christ does not merely arrange peace between parties; he is the substance in which peace consists. Peace is a person, and apart from him there is no other source of it.

“The dividing wall of hostility” almost certainly alludes to the stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple beyond which Gentiles could not pass under penalty of death — inscription fragments have been found. Christ abolished it “in his flesh”: the physical reality of his crucified body is what dismantled the theological barrier.

“One new man” (hena kainon anthropon) — not Gentiles absorbed into Judaism, not a cultural compromise, but a third entity that is genuinely unprecedented. The gospel does not baptise either culture; it creates a new one.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reconciliation is first vertical (to God) and then horizontal (Jew and Gentile). The sequence is theologically precise: you cannot have the horizontal without the vertical. Purely social gospels attempt the horizontal reconciliation without dealing with the underlying problem — alienation from God — and therefore cannot produce lasting unity. The cross solves the root issue; the human reconciliation flows from that solution.

“Killing the hostility” — the same cross that kills sin kills the enmity between peoples. The violence that was directed at Christ absorbs the violence that divided humanity.

verseByVerse.quote: For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Access” (prosagōgê) is the word for the right of approach to a king — being formally ushered into the royal presence. Jew and Gentile now stand before the Father through the same Christ and in the same Spirit. The Trinity is the architecture of inclusion: access is through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary: Three images of belonging converge in rapid succession: citizens of a city, members of a household, stones in a building — each one a reversal of the Gentile exclusion catalogued in v. 12. “So then” (ara oun) gathers everything: the distance, the cross, the peace, the access — and resolves it into a new identity. “No longer strangers and aliens” — the precise vocabulary of exclusion from v. 12 is reversed. Now they are fellow citizens with the saints — same city, same rights, same access to the throne of grace. And members of the household of God — not guests but family. Verse 20 grounds the belonging: this community is built on the apostolic foundation, the authoritative word entrusted to the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone — the stone that determines the alignment of every other stone. Calvin: “The foundation of the apostles and prophets is the doctrine they preached; to move away from it is to destroy the whole building.” (cf. 1 Cor. 3:11; 1 Pet. 2:4–6)

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: The temple image is the climax of the chapter. Paul moves from citizenship to family to temple — and the building is not made of stone but of persons. “Grows” (auxei) — the church is not a static monument but a living, organic structure still under construction. The growth is upward: into a holy temple in the Lord, culminating in a dwelling place for God by the Spirit. This is the reversal of exile: God displaced from his temple and his people, now building a new and permanent dwelling in redeemed humanity. Stott notes the stunning convergence: in v. 21 the whole structure grows; in v. 22 you are being built together — the cosmic and the personal are one. The same Spirit who descended at Pentecost fits living stones together into a habitation for the living God.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins to pray and then stops himself. "For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—" and then the sentence breaks off, swallowed by a parenthesis that doesn't resolve until v.14. He cannot proceed to the prayer without first explaining the stewardship that has brought him to prison — because the mystery he has been entrusted to proclaim is itself the reason for the prayer, and the prayer only makes sense in light of the mystery. Paul is constitutionally unable to speak of anything without grounding it in the gospel.

The mystery he describes is one of the most world-altering disclosures in all of Scripture. "The Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel" (v.6). In the Old Testament, the Gentiles were at the periphery of God's purposes — they could be blessed through Israel, they could join themselves to Israel, but they were not Israel. Now the secret is out: the wall was always meant to come down. The distinction was always meant to be temporary, a pedagogy pointing toward its own dissolution. In Christ, there are no second-class citizens of the Kingdom, no Gentiles-in-the-anteroom. Fellow heirs. Fellow members. Fellow partakers. The same body. The same promise.

And the disclosure of this mystery has dimensions that exceed the merely human. "Through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (v.10). The angels are watching the church. The principalities and powers — the spiritual intelligences that inhabit the heavenly realm — are learning the wisdom of God by observing the community of the redeemed. The church is God's cosmic classroom. When a Jew and a Gentile, a slave and a free person, a man and a woman sit together at the Lord's table — the universe sees something it could not have deduced by any other means: the manifold, many-coloured, inexhaustible wisdom of a God who makes all things new.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul begins to pray — “for this reason” picks up the cosmic reconciliation of chapter 2 — and immediately interrupts himself with a parenthesis that will not close until v. 13. He cannot speak of the mystery without first explaining his own role in it. But before the explanation, he names himself plainly: “I, Paul.” And “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” — not Rome’s prisoner, though he sits in chains. His imprisonment is not defeat but vocation, the cost of proclaiming the mystery to the Gentiles. He belongs entirely to Christ, and it is on their behalf that he wears these chains. Calvin: “The very chains of Paul are more to be glorified than all the triumphs of kings.”

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Stewardship” (oikonomia) — the same word used in 1:10 for God’s own plan. Paul’s apostleship is not self-appointed; it is a trust of divine grace entrusted to him for others. Everything he has comes as gift and responsibility. The mystery was “made known to me by revelation” — not by study or tradition but by direct divine disclosure on the Damascus road (Gal 1:12). Paul has written about this briefly (as in Gal and Rom); his readers know the outline. What follows in vv. 4–13 is not new information but a deeper sounding of what they already hold.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Not made known… as it has now been revealed” — the mystery was not absent from the Old Testament but it was hidden there, not yet visible. The apostles and prophets together form the revelatory foundation of the church (2:20). Their office was unrepeatable: once the revelation was complete and inscripturated, the foundation was laid and does not need to be relaid. This is why claims to new apostolic revelation are theologically incoherent in Paul’s own terms. (cf. Col. 1:26–27; Rom. 16:25–26)

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the same promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three “fellow-” compounds in Greek (sug-klêronomos, sus-sōma, sum-metocha), each insisting on equal standing. Fellow heirs — same inheritance. Same body — not a parallel body, the same one. Same promise — not derivative promises, the original covenant promise. The equality is absolute, and it comes “through the gospel” — the proclaimed word is the instrument of inclusion, not circumcision or Torah-keeping.

verseByVerse.quote: To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The very least of all the saints” — in Greek Paul coins a new comparative form of “least” (elachistoteros) to go below what Greek grammar allows. He is not performing false modesty; he is referencing the fact that he persecuted the church (1 Cor. 15:9). The grace that reached him is the most dramatic exhibit in the letter of what he is describing.

“Unsearchable” (anexichniastos) — literally untraceable, incapable of being tracked to its source. The riches of Christ exceed every map. No theology can exhaust them; no lifetime of preaching can deplete them.

verseByVerse.quote: So that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is not merely the beneficiary of the mystery; it is the medium of its announcement to the cosmos. “Manifold” (polupoikilos) — many-coloured, richly varied, like an intricate mosaic. The wisdom of God is displayed in its full complexity through the multi-ethnic, multi-cultural unity of the church.

The rulers and authorities in the heavenly places are watching the church. They are watching not because the church is impressive but because the thing visible in it — the impossible unity of former enemies at one table — is the clearest display in the cosmos of what God’s wisdom looks like deployed at full scale.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cosmic sermon preached through the church (v. 10) flows from God’s “eternal purpose” (prothesis tōn aiōnōn — the purpose of the ages). Everything in redemptive history, including the church’s formation and mission, was planned in the mind of God before time and has now been realized — brought to its telos — in Christ Jesus our Lord. The consequence for every believer is bold access: parrēsia (the right of free speech before a ruler) and prosagōgē (the right of approach to a king), both held with confidence through faith in him. Access that no Gentile could have imagined in the old age is now the daily possession of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parenthesis closes with a pastoral stroke: do not be discouraged on my account. Paul’s sufferings are not evidence that the mystery has stalled or that God has abandoned his plan — they are “your glory,” the price of Gentile inclusion in the people of God. What looks like defeat (apostle in prison) is actually fulfillment: the chains are the cost of the Gentiles’ inheritance. Keller: “The suffering of the servant is not an interruption of the mission — it is often the very means by which the mission advances.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul falls to his knees. He began to pray in v.1 and was swept away by the parenthesis of his own apostolic calling. Now, in v.14, he returns to his knees — and what follows is the most doxologically charged prayer in the New Testament. Four requests of escalating grandeur, each one building on the last, until the whole structure reaches a summit it cannot contain and erupts into one of the greatest doxologies ever written. The prayer is a mountain, and at its peak the clouds part.

He prays first for inner strengthening by the Spirit in the inner person — the deep, hidden, interior part of the human being where the real life is lived. He prays then for Christ to dwell in the heart by faith — not merely to visit, but to take up permanent residence, to be at home there. He prays third for the comprehension of something incomprehensible: the breadth and length and height and depth of the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge. Four dimensions — suggesting something that cannot be measured in any direction, a love that exceeds every capacity to contain or categorise it. And then, the goal that gathers all of this up: "that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." The finite vessel of the human soul invited to receive the infinite fullness of the divine life.

The doxology that follows (vv.20–21) is the most expansive statement of God's power to answer prayer in all of Scripture: He is able to do "far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us." The Greek accumulates superlatives: "above all," "abundantly above all," "exceeding abundantly above all" — language stacking on language, because language cannot contain what Paul wants to say about the inexhaustible capacity of God to exceed every prayer and every imagination. We always pray too small. God always answers beyond the asking. The prayer ends where the letter began: to Him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. John Calvin commented that Paul "had no measure in his desires" for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust His capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun His willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which He does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; His answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation.
