The purpose of this love is the wife’s sanctification and eventual glorification (vv. 26–27) — the husband investing in her holiness through word, prayer, and attentive presence; holding before her a truer picture of who she is in Christ than the voices she grew up with. The one-flesh reality of v. 31 deepens this: what is done to her is done to him. Her flourishing is inseparable from his own — so he attends to her the way he attends to pain in his own body: promptly, because she is part of him.

“One flesh” means a comprehensive, covenantal union: physical (sexual union as covenant sign), relational (lives genuinely intertwined, interests no longer separable), covenantal (permanent, witnessed by God, Mal. 2:14), and exclusive (one man, one woman, one union). What it does not mean: the loss of individual identity, perfect harmony without conflict, the superseding of all other relationships, or a reality achieved instantly. The leaving and the holding-fast of Gen. 2:24 are active and ongoing: a daily re-election of the spouse above all others.

The section closes with the double summary of v. 33: the husband loves, the wife respects. These are not identical but complementary — each addressed at the point of their deepest calling and their deepest vulnerability. And each is a daily practice long before it is a feeling: the husband who consistently turns toward his wife’s need, and the wife who consistently honours her husband’s leadership, are enacting the gospel in the most ordinary moments of married life — and the watching world sees something it cannot produce on its own.

The household code tradition (Haustafeln): Paul engages a well-established literary genre — Aristotle, the Stoics, Hellenistic Jewish writers all taught household management through three pairs: husband/wife, parent/child, master/slave. Paul uses the same structure but transforms it radically: he addresses the subordinate party first (giving them full moral standing as agents accountable to Christ); grounds every command in Christ rather than nature or social utility; gives the longer and more demanding command to the dominant party; and embeds the entire code in mutual submission (v. 21). The form is conventional; the content is a quiet revolution.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over His church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: "as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who "came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to "submit to your own husband, as to the Lord" (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb “submit” is not present in the Greek of v. 22 — it carries over from the mutual submission of v. 21 (hypotassomenoi). Wives are called to the same posture Paul has just called every believer to adopt toward one another, applied in the specific relation to their own husbands. “As to the Lord” — not because the husband is divine, but because the wife’s submission is ultimately an act of obedience to Christ who has ordered marriage this way. The husband’s authority is borrowed and bounded; the wife’s submission is given to God himself through this divinely appointed structure.

What submission means. The Greek hypotassō was a military term: to arrange oneself under the authority of another, to recognise an ordering. It is a voluntary, willing act — not forced compliance but a free choice to honour the structure God has established. Paul is not speaking of worth or intelligence or spiritual standing — Galatians 3:28 is clear that in Christ there is neither male nor female in terms of standing before God. He is speaking of role within the covenant of marriage, just as within the Trinity the Son submits to the Father without being in any way inferior to him (1 Cor. 11:3; 15:28). The pattern of submission within equality is written into the very life of God.

Submission in marriage means the wife voluntarily honours her husband’s God-given leadership role — supporting his decisions, deferring to his direction in the ordering of the household, and doing so not grudgingly but as a gift freely given. It is a posture of trust, not of passivity. The submitted wife is not a silent, opinionless presence; she brings her full wisdom, gifts, and voice to the marriage, and a good husband depends on that. But when decisions must be made and agreement cannot be reached, she trusts the structure God has given rather than insisting on her own way.

What submission does not mean. Paul is careful, and so must the preacher be:

  • It does not mean the wife is inferior. Submission is a role, not a rank. The Son is not less than the Father; he submits to the Father’s will freely and gloriously. A wife who submits to her husband is not diminished; she is reflecting the Trinitarian pattern of love-within-order. cf. 1 Cor. 11:3.
  • It does not mean blind obedience to sin. The qualifier is “as to the Lord.” If a husband asks his wife to sin, to lie, to participate in something that violates God’s clear commands, the wife’s first loyalty is to Christ. Acts 5:29: “we must obey God rather than men.” Submission is to a husband who is himself under Christ’s authority; it does not require complicity in sin or the violation of conscience.
  • It does not mean enduring abuse. Nothing in this passage requires a wife to remain in a situation of physical danger or sustained abuse. The entire framework of Ephesians 5 is mutual self-giving love, not domination. A husband who abuses his wife is not exercising biblical headship; he is violating it catastrophically. The church has a responsibility to protect, not to bind.
  • It does not mean the wife has no voice. Proverbs 31 describes the noble wife as a woman of enormous competence, initiative, and influence. The submitted wife of Ephesians 5 is not silenced; she is secure enough in the structure to speak freely, knowing that her husband is charged with her good (vv. 25–29).
  • It does not mean this is a burden uniquely borne by the wife. The command to submit comes immediately after the command to all believers to submit to one another (v. 21). And what follows is the far longer and weightier charge to the husband: love your wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (v. 25). If the wife is called to submit, the husband is called to die. The greater burden, by any honest measure, falls on the husband.

What this looks like in practice — three examples:

  • A decision about where to live. A husband is offered a significant career opportunity in another city. The wife is deeply reluctant — her relationships, her work, her elderly parents are all where they are. They discuss it fully and honestly; she shares her concerns clearly and he listens carefully. He still believes they should go. Submission here means she trusts his judgment, follows his lead, and does not allow the decision to become a permanent grievance. She is not overruled without voice; she is choosing to trust the structure after her voice has been fully heard. He, for his part, carries the weight of that decision and owes her every sacrifice to make it work.
  • A daily pattern of honour rather than competition. Submission is not only visible in big decisions; it shows in daily tone. The wife who does not routinely undermine her husband’s leadership in front of the children, who speaks well of him to others, who defers publicly even when she privately disagrees — is practising submission in the texture of ordinary life. It is the disposition, not just the dramatic moment.
  • A theological disagreement. A wife is more theologically astute than her husband and knows it. He holds a view she believes is mistaken. Submission does not mean she pretends to agree or withholds her wisdom. She speaks clearly, shares her reasoning, even presses the point. But she does so as a partner who respects his role, not as a competitor who needs to win. If he is unmoved and the matter is not one of clear sin, she defers — trusting that the God who established this structure is capable of leading her husband without her needing to override him.

cf. 1 Pet. 3:1–6, where Peter grounds the wife’s submission in the same pattern — voluntary, Christ-directed, inwardly free — and holds up Sarah as the model: a woman of strength who called Abraham “lord” not out of fear but out of faith. Col. 3:18: “wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.”

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grounds the husband’s headship in the analogy of Christ’s headship over the church — and this analogy both establishes and radically reshapes the authority it grants. Christ is head and Savior; he gave himself for the church, nourishes and cherishes it (v. 29). Headship is servant-leadership, cross-shaped from the start. “His body” — the church is not beneath Christ but united to him, inseparable. “In everything” does not mean blind obedience without limit — the analogy itself provides the limit: the church submits to Christ, not to anyone who contradicts him. No human husband may command what the Lord forbids.

What the husband’s headship means. The word kephalē — head — in Paul’s usage carries the sense of source, sustainer, and servant-leader, always shaped by the Christ-analogy he himself provides. Christ’s headship over the church is not domination; it is the headship of one who “gave himself up for her” (v. 25), who nourishes and cherishes the body as his own flesh (v. 29), who sanctifies and cleanses her (v. 26). This is the only model Paul offers for the husband’s headship. It means:

  • Taking ultimate responsibility. The head bears the weight of the household — spiritually, practically, relationally. When things go wrong, the husband does not look for someone to blame; he asks what he failed to do or should have done differently. Adam’s failure in Genesis 3 was precisely this: he was present, silent, and passive when he should have led (Gen. 3:6). God came looking for Adam first (Gen. 3:9) — because the head is held accountable.
  • Initiating love, not waiting for it. The head sets the tone. A husband who waits for his wife to create the emotional warmth of the marriage, who responds rather than initiates, who is present physically but absent spiritually — is abdicating headship. Christ did not wait for the church to love him first; he loved while we were still enemies (Rom. 5:8). The husband’s love leads.
  • Spiritual leadership of the household. The head prays with and for his wife. He takes initiative in the spiritual formation of the home. He ensures the family is rooted in the word, in the church, in prayer. He does not delegate this to his wife and call it her department. It is his calling first.
  • Servant-shaped decision-making. When the husband leads in decision-making, he does so having genuinely listened, having sought his wife’s wisdom, having weighed her concerns as heavily as his own. The decision he makes should demonstrably take her good into account — not “I lead therefore I decide” but “I lead therefore I bear the cost of this for her sake.”

What headship does not mean.

  • It does not mean the husband makes every decision unilaterally. Headship is not a licence for autocracy. The wise husband actively draws on his wife’s wisdom, defers to her competence in areas where she knows more, and makes many decisions together. Headship is about ultimate accountability and direction, not the micromanagement of every choice.
  • It does not mean the husband is spiritually superior. The wife may be more mature in faith, more gifted in discernment, more disciplined in prayer. Headship is a role, not a certificate of spiritual achievement. A humble husband recognises his wife’s gifts and is enriched by them.
  • It does not mean the husband’s word overrides Scripture. His authority is entirely derivative — borrowed from Christ, bounded by Christ, answerable to Christ. A husband who uses headship language to exempt himself from accountability, to suppress his wife’s conscience, or to avoid the hard work of genuine partnership, has turned a servant’s calling into a tyrant’s convenience.
  • It does not mean silence from the wife. The head needs the body to function. A husband who cannot hear challenge, who responds to his wife’s honest disagreement as a threat to his authority, is not exercising headship — he is protecting his ego. Christ is not threatened by the church’s prayers and questions; he invites them.
  • It is not a position of comfort but of cost. The head goes first into difficulty. He sacrifices his preferences, his comfort, his ambitions for the flourishing of his wife and household. If he is eating well while she is struggling, resting while she is exhausted, pursuing his own interests while hers are unmet — he is not leading; he is being served.

A real-life example. David and his wife Claire have been married for twelve years. Claire has carried most of the emotional weight of raising their three children while David has focused on building his career. He is not unkind — he provides well, is rarely harsh, loves his family. But he is largely absent from the spiritual life of the home. He does not pray with Claire. He does not lead the children in any form of family devotion. When Claire raises hard topics — her loneliness, her exhaustion, a growing distance between them — David listens for a few minutes and then moves the conversation on. He calls this “not being the type to overanalyse things.”

By the standard of Ephesians 5, David is not exercising headship; he is occupying the position without bearing the cost. He has the authority but not the responsibility. The headship Paul describes would look different: David initiates a conversation about their marriage before Claire has to raise it again. He admits he has been absent and names it as his failure. He begins to pray with Claire — awkwardly at first, briefly, but deliberately. He asks her what she needs from him spiritually and acts on the answer. He makes choices that protect her time and replenish her rather than assuming she will manage. None of this requires a dramatic personality change; it requires the decision to lead as Christ leads — by turning toward rather than away, by giving rather than taking, by bearing the weight rather than distributing it.

This is the headship Paul has in mind: not a crown to be claimed but a cross to be carried. cf. 1 Pet. 3:7: “husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way… showing honour to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.” Col. 3:19: “husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.”

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband receives the longer and more demanding instruction. His love is measured by the cross. The verb is agapaō — self-giving covenant love, not sentiment. “As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” — this is the standard: the willingness to give oneself completely for the good of the beloved, at the cost of everything. Paul does not say “lead your wives” first; he says “love your wives.” The leadership is shaped entirely by the love; the authority exists to serve the beloved’s flourishing, not to assert itself. (cf. Col. 3:19; 1 Pet. 3:7)

What this looks like in real life. The standard — love as Christ loved — can feel so towering that it becomes abstract. Paul is describing a daily marriage, not a theological ideal. Here is what cross-shaped love looks like in the ordinary week:

  • He notices what she carries and moves to relieve it — without being asked. She has had a hard week with the children. He sees it. He does not wait for her to say she is exhausted; he takes over the evening without comment, puts the children to bed, and makes sure she has time to breathe. Christ did not wait for the church to articulate her need; he saw the condition and acted. The husband who is paying attention to his wife — genuinely watching, genuinely present — will find a hundred small opportunities to give himself up for her every week.
  • He sacrifices his preferences for hers, consistently and cheerfully. He would rather spend Saturday morning the way he wants to spend it. She needs something different from him — time together, a conversation, help with a project she has been asking about. He gives up his preference without martyrdom, without the pointed silence that makes her feel guilty for asking. This is not occasional heroism; it is the steady, unglamorous daily giving of himself that Paul has in view. Any man can sacrifice once in a crisis. The question is whether the pattern of ordinary days shows a man who is consistently moving toward his wife rather than away.
  • He takes her spiritual wellbeing seriously. Christ gave himself for the church “that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word” (v. 26). The husband who loves as Christ loves is invested in his wife’s spiritual health — not as a supervisor of her godliness, but as a man who prays for her, who asks how she is doing with God, who makes it easy for her to attend church and be part of community, who chooses the kind of life together that feeds her faith rather than starving it. He is not passive about this. He initiates.
  • He chooses her above his career, his hobbies, and his comfort, when they conflict. A promotion requires travel four days a week for two years. It would advance his career significantly. But his wife is struggling, their marriage is thin, their children need him. Cross-shaped love asks: what does she need? What does this family need? And it is willing to give the answer, even if the answer is costly. Christ did not choose his own comfort over the church’s need. The husband who habitually chooses his own flourishing at the expense of his wife’s is not exercising headship; he is reversing it.
  • He asks for forgiveness — specifically and promptly. He was sharp with her this morning. He knew it the moment the words came out. The cross-shaped husband does not let it sit, does not rationalise it away, does not wait for her to bring it up. He goes to her and says: “I was unkind this morning and I am sorry. Will you forgive me?” No qualifications, no “but you also…” This small act, repeated over years, builds a marriage in which she knows she is safe with him — that when he fails her he will not defend himself but will return to her. That security is itself a form of giving himself up for her.

None of these examples requires extraordinary character or unusual gifts. They require only the decision, made again each day, to orient the day around her flourishing rather than his own comfort. This is what “gave himself up” means when it is translated from the cross into a kitchen, a bedroom, a difficult conversation on a Tuesday evening. The cross was a single event; its pattern is a lifelong daily practice. cf. 1 Cor. 13:4–7; 1 Pet. 3:7.

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose of Christ’s self-giving is the church’s sanctification and final glorification. “The washing of water with the word” — the external sign of baptism and the proclaimed gospel work together. Christ’s purpose for his bride is holiness — progressive now, perfect at the last. “Present the church to himself in splendor” — the imagery of the radiant bride at the wedding, every blemish removed by his own atoning work. The husband who loves like Christ sets before himself not a program of control but a vision of his wife’s holiness and flourishing as the telos of his entire life with her. Stott: “No husband has loved his wife as Christ has loved the church; but this remains the standard toward which all Christian husbands strive.”

What this looks like in real life. Marcus has been married to Priya for eight years. Priya grew up in a home where faith was nominal and her self-image was quietly eroded by a critical father. She came to Christ in her mid-twenties, but old patterns still surface: she dismisses her own gifts, struggles to believe she is truly loved by God, and finds it hard to receive praise without deflecting it.

Marcus has noticed. Slowly, over years, he has made it his quiet mission to speak truth into these specific places. When Priya dismisses a gift she has, he does not let it pass — he names what he sees in her, specifically, not generically. When she doubts God’s love after a hard season, he opens Scripture with her and walks through what it says, not to win an argument but to wash her with the word. He prays over her by name, for the specific fears and lies she has named to him. He has chosen, deliberately, to remember the things that shame her and to speak against them — not to fix her but to serve her sanctification.

He is not her therapist or her pastor. He is her husband. But in the ordinary texture of their life together, he is doing what Christ does for the church: cleansing with the word, moving her toward the person God made her to be, holding before her a vision of who she is in Christ that is truer than the voice she grew up with. That is the husband who “sanctifies” in Paul’s sense — not by spiritual authority over her, but by the daily, attentive, word-saturated love that helps her become more fully herself in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul shifts from the Christological standard to the creational reality: in marriage, the two become one flesh (v. 31, citing Gen 2:24). Therefore to love the wife is to love what is, in a profound sense, oneself. This is not narcissism but the logic of union: the husband who nurtures and cares for his wife is tending the one-flesh reality that includes himself. The converse is equally true: the husband who neglects or wounds his wife injures himself. The union created in marriage is so real that what is done to one is done to both.

What this looks like in real life. The logic of one-flesh love exposes something most husbands understand instinctively about their own bodies but rarely apply to their wives. A man does not ignore a pain in his shoulder because he is busy. He does not dismiss his own hunger because it is inconvenient. He does not tell his own body it is being too sensitive when it signals distress. He attends to it, responds to it, takes it seriously — because it is his.

Paul says: do the same for your wife. James has been so absorbed in a demanding work season that he has not noticed Sarah pulling back emotionally for three weeks. She has been quieter at dinner, slower to reach for him, carrying something he has not asked about. He tells himself she is fine, that he will check in when the pressure eases. But he would never apply that reasoning to a pain in his own chest. He would not wait until a convenient moment to attend to something wrong in his own body.

The one-flesh reality Paul describes means that Sarah’s withdrawal is James’s signal. Her heaviness is his concern. Her flourishing is inseparable from his own. The husband who grasps this stops asking “is she okay?” as a rhetorical question and starts asking it as a real one — and then waits for the real answer. He turns toward what he notices in her the way he turns toward what he notices in himself: promptly, attentively, because she is not separate from him but part of him. cf. Gen. 2:24; 1 Cor. 7:3–4.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Nourishes” (ektrephei) and “cherishes” (thalpei — literally, to warm) — the language of tender, careful provision. Paul’s point: self-care is natural and instinctive; no one destroys their own body. Marriage extends this instinct to the wife who is, in the mystery of one flesh, the husband’s own body. And the analogy returns to Christ: he nourishes and cherishes the church because “we are members of his body.” The church is not external to Christ but united to him in a union the cross created and the Spirit maintains. The husband’s tenderness toward his wife is thus patterned on the most patient and self-giving love in existence.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 — the creation charter of marriage, spoken by God before the fall, before sin entered, before the distortions that have plagued every marriage since. This is what marriage was always meant to be: a leaving, a cleaving, a becoming one. Three movements, each essential.

What “one flesh” means. The phrase is rich and multi-layered. It is not merely a poetic way of describing sexual union, though it includes that. One flesh in the biblical sense describes a comprehensive, covenantal union of two persons that is irreversible in its nature, total in its scope, and exclusive in its loyalty.

  • It is physical. Sexual union is the God-ordained sign and consummation of the one-flesh covenant. This is why Paul can say in 1 Corinthians 6:16 that even union with a prostitute makes one flesh — the act is designed by God to seal a permanent covenant, and when it occurs outside that covenant it does damage precisely because it enacts what is not there. Sex in Scripture is never merely recreational; it is covenantal, and it carries that weight whether the participants acknowledge it or not.
  • It is relational and emotional. One flesh means the two lives are now genuinely intertwined. What happens to one happens to both. His failure affects her; her suffering is his. There is no clean separation of interests any more. The husband who says “that’s her problem” about his wife’s distress has not understood what he became when he married her.
  • It is spiritual and covenantal. Marriage in Scripture is a covenant (Mal. 2:14: “she is your companion and your wife by covenant”), witnessed by God and binding in his sight. The one-flesh union is not dissolved by distance, disappointment, or the fading of feeling. It is a permanent bond created by a public, sworn commitment — which is why its violation by adultery is so serious, and why its dissolution by divorce is always a tearing of what God joined.
  • It is exclusive. “His wife” — one man, one woman, one union. The one-flesh reality cannot be shared across multiple partners without being fundamentally destroyed. This is the ground of the Bible’s insistence on sexual faithfulness within marriage and its equal insistence on the wrongness of sexual union outside it.

What “one flesh” does not mean.

  • It does not mean the loss of individual identity. The two become one but they do not cease to be two. Each person retains their distinct personality, gifts, calling, and relationship with God. A wife is not absorbed into her husband; a husband does not lose himself into his wife. The union is a new reality that includes and enriches both persons — it does not erase them. A marriage in which one person dominates or subsumes the other is not a picture of one flesh; it is a distortion of it.
  • It does not mean perfect harmony at all times. The two are genuinely one, but they are still two sinners in a fallen world. One flesh does not produce automatic agreement, the absence of conflict, or the end of individual struggle. What it produces is a shared life in which the conflicts and struggles are faced together rather than separately — which is something far better than the absence of difficulty.
  • It does not mean the marriage relationship supersedes all others absolutely. The command to “leave father and mother” establishes that marriage creates a new primary loyalty — but it does not eliminate other loyalties. Both husband and wife retain responsibilities to parents, children, the church, and the wider community. One flesh means the marriage bond is primary among human relationships, not that it is the only one.
  • It is not achieved instantly or automatically. The legal and covenantal union is created at the wedding. The experienced reality of one flesh — the deep knowing, the intertwining of lives, the trust that allows full vulnerability — is built over years of choosing each other. Many couples are legally one flesh and experientially distant. The calling of marriage is to close that gap, day by day, until the legal reality and the lived experience match.

The “leaving” and “holding fast” that Paul quotes from Genesis are equally important. Leaving means the primary loyalty genuinely shifts: a man who is still emotionally or functionally controlled by his parents after marriage has not yet left, whatever the geographical distance. Holding fast (proskollaō — to be glued to, bonded) means the active, ongoing choosing of the spouse above all others — a daily re-election that no amount of familiarity or disappointment is permitted to dissolve. cf. Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:5–6; 1 Cor. 6:16–17; Mal. 2:14–16.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul makes a breathtaking hermeneutical claim: the mystērion embedded in Genesis 2:24 has always referred to Christ and the church. The leaving and cleaving, the one-flesh union — all of it has been a sign pointing beyond itself to the union of the incarnate Son with the humanity he came to save. This does not make marriage less real; it makes it more glorious. Every faithful marriage is a living icon of the gospel: the self-giving of Christ for his bride, the response of the church in love and trust. The mystery hidden in Genesis 2 has been disclosed in Ephesians 5. cf. Gen. 2:24; Rev. 19:7–9; Hos. 2:19–20.

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soaring theology resolves into immediate, personal application: each one, his wife, her husband — the singular weight of it. Love (agapaō) for the husband; respect (phobos — reverence, honor) for the wife. These are not identical but complementary. The husband’s deepest need is to be respected; the wife’s deepest need is to be loved. Paul addresses each at the point of their calling and their vulnerability. “As himself” — self-love is the measure; the husband who cares for his wife with the same attention he gives to his own wellbeing has understood what the one-flesh union requires of him.

An example for the husband. Tom and Rachel have been married for fifteen years. Tom works hard and provides well, but his emotional language is sparse. He is not cold, but he rarely initiates affection, rarely says “I love you” unless Rachel says it first, and tends to respond to her emotional needs with practical solutions rather than presence. Rachel has told him more than once that she feels unseen. Tom has heard it, nodded, and carried on much the same.

Paul’s word lands here with personal weight: each one of you love his wife as himself. Tom does not neglect his own hunger, his own tiredness, his own need for respect at work. He responds to those needs promptly and naturally. The command is to transfer that same attentiveness to Rachel. Practically, for Tom, this means learning to ask and stay — not “are you okay?” but “tell me how you’re actually doing” and then sitting with the answer rather than fixing it. It means initiating affection before she has to signal her need for it. It means noticing when she is carrying something and naming it: “you seem heavy today — what’s going on?” None of this requires Tom to become a different person. It requires him to apply to his wife the same care he already applies, instinctively, to himself. That is the measure Paul gives him.

An example for the wife. Nina’s husband Daniel leads a small team at work and carries significant responsibility. At home, Nina has a sharper mind for detail and is usually right when they disagree. Over the years, a pattern has formed: she corrects him in front of the children, sighs when he makes a decision she thinks is suboptimal, and occasionally makes a joke at his expense with friends — affectionately, she tells herself, but Daniel has gone quiet when it happens more than once. He has not said anything. But Nina has noticed he volunteers less at home, defers to her on more decisions than he used to, and seems to have stopped trying to lead.

Paul’s word to the wife is phobos — not fear but reverence and honour. The man who is respected by his wife at home is freed to lead; the man who is regularly diminished retreats. For Nina, respect in practice means catching the correction before it reaches her lips in public and saving it for a private moment. It means letting Daniel make a decision she thinks is slightly wrong — when the stakes are not serious — and not revisiting it. It means saying, in front of the children, something genuinely admiring about him — not flattery but the truth she actually believes about him, spoken where he can hear it landed. It means noticing when he has led well and naming it: “that was a good call.” Respect, like love, is less a feeling than a practice — a daily series of small choices to honour the man she married, not because he has earned every honour, but because God has called her to it and because Daniel, like every human being, becomes more of what he is told he is.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit-filled community of 5:18–21, expressed in the marriage covenant of 5:22–33, now extends into the full household: children and parents, servants and masters. These are not grand or glamorous relationships — they are the daily, ordinary, sometimes tedious texture of domestic life. And yet Paul charges every one of them with gospel significance. The Spirit who fills the worshipping community also fills the kitchen, the nursery, the workshop, the field. There is no space in the Christian household that is exempt from the Lordship of Christ, no relationship that lies outside the sanctifying reach of the gospel.

The commands are given with careful balance. Children are told to obey — but fathers are immediately told not to provoke. Servants are told to serve faithfully — but masters are immediately told to treat their servants with justice and fairness. In every pair, both parties receive commands; in every pair, both parties are accountable to Christ. This symmetry is itself a theological statement: in the household of the Spirit-filled community, no one is merely the recipient of others' service and no one is merely the dispenser of commands. All are servants of Christ, all are accountable to the same Lord, all are engaged in the same vocation of making their ordinary relationships a theatre of God's glory.

The motivating principle that runs through the entire passage is Paul's repeated phrase "as to the Lord" or "as slaves of Christ." The child who obeys parents is obeying "in the Lord" (v.1). The servant who works faithfully does so "as to the Lord and not to men" (v.7). The master treats servants justly "knowing that he also has a Master in heaven" (v.9). Every human authority is relativised by a higher authority; every human service is dignified by being rendered to Christ. The gospel transforms every relationship in the household not by changing its external form but by changing the motivation, the orientation, and the significance of everything done within it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. "Obey... as you would Christ," "doing the will of God from the heart," "rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord." Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — "do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him" (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord" and "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary: “In the Lord” qualifies and deepens the obedience: children obey not merely because parents have authority but because Christ is Lord of the household and has ordered it this way. “This is right” (dikaion estin) — not merely commanded but fitting, consistent with the created order and the moral structure of the family. Paul addresses children directly — they are full members of the congregation, present when the letter is read aloud, accountable to Christ for their own response to his word. The qualifier “in the Lord” also provides the limit: obedience is within the scope of the Lord’s own commands, not extending to what Christ himself forbids. (cf. Col. 3:20; Prov. 1:8)

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reaches to the fifth commandment (Exod. 20:12; Deut. 5:16) and notes its distinction: it carries a promise. “Honour” (timē) is broader than childhood obedience — it encompasses the ongoing respect, care, and esteem owed to parents through adult life. The promise of well-being and longevity reflects a wisdom God has built into human community: the generation that honours parents sustains the social fabric across time. The commandment outlasts the household; it shapes the posture of the grown child toward aging parents long after direct obedience is no longer the primary mode of the relationship.

What honouring father and mother means.

  • Speaking of them with respect. How an adult child speaks about their parents — to their spouse, their own children, their friends — is itself a form of honour or dishonour. Recounting their failures as entertainment, reducing them to their worst moments, or performing therapy on their inadequacies in every conversation, dishonours them even if everything said is factually true. Honour means choosing what to say and how to say it with their dignity in mind.
  • Treating them with consistent courtesy. The parent who is growing older, slower, more repetitive, less capable — still holds the position of father or mother. Honour means patience with their limitations, attentiveness to their needs, and the refusal to treat them as a burden to be managed. The tone of voice used with aging parents is itself a measure of honour.
  • Practical care in old age. Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for using “Corban” — declaring resources as offered to God — to exempt themselves from caring for aging parents (Mark 7:9–13). He called it making void the word of God. 1 Timothy 5:8 makes the obligation explicit: a person who does not provide for their own household “has denied the faith.” Honour in practice means being willing to spend time, money, and energy on parents who can no longer care fully for themselves — not delegating it entirely to institutions because it is inconvenient.
  • Listening to their wisdom. Proverbs 23:22: “listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.” Even imperfect parents have decades of lived experience worth hearing. The adult child who consistently dismisses parental input without genuine consideration is not honouring. Honour includes the posture of a learner, even when one knows more in certain areas.
  • Including them in family life. Grandparents honoured by their children are present at family meals, involved with grandchildren, consulted and included. The parent who is quietly sidelined from the new family — only invited at Christmas, never asked for advice, kept at managed distance — is not being honoured. Honour has a warmth and an openness to it that mere obligation lacks.

What honouring father and mother does not mean.

  • It does not mean blind obedience in adulthood. Once a child is grown, the primary relationship changes. Paul has already established in Ephesians 5:31 that marriage creates a new primary loyalty — a man leaves his father and mother. An adult who cannot make a major decision about their own home, career, or marriage without parental approval has not yet left. Honouring parents does not mean remaining permanently under their direction. It means respecting their role while exercising adult responsibility for one’s own life.
  • It does not mean tolerating or covering sin. If a parent is abusive, addicted, or persistently harmful, honour does not require the adult child to pretend otherwise or to expose themselves or their children to ongoing damage. Honour is compatible with appropriate boundaries. The child who sets a boundary with a destructive parent — calmly, without contempt, for the sake of their own household — is not dishonoring. Honour and self-protection are not mutually exclusive.
  • It does not mean placing parents above a spouse. The new primary loyalty of marriage means that honouring parents cannot come at the cost of the marriage covenant. An adult who consistently sides with a parent against their spouse, who shares marital confidences with parents, or who allows parents to undermine the marriage, is not honouring marriage or parents rightly. Both relationships are to be honoured — but in their proper order.
  • It does not mean pretending a difficult relationship is fine. Some adult children carry real wounds from their parents. Honouring does not require denial of that reality, forced warmth that is not genuine, or the suppression of honest conversation about harm done. Honour can coexist with honesty, grief, and the slow work of forgiveness — but it means pursuing the relationship with goodwill rather than contempt.

Practical examples.

  • Honouring in practice: Emma’s mother has become increasingly forgetful and asks the same questions in every phone call. Emma has a busy household and finds the calls draining. But she calls every week, listens patiently, answers the repeated question without sarcasm, and once a month drives two hours to spend the day with her mother in person. She does not speak of her mother’s decline with impatience in front of her own children. She has decided that how she treats her mother is teaching her children how they will one day treat her.
  • Not honouring in practice: Rob’s father was a hard man and their relationship carries old wounds. At family gatherings Rob retells the same stories of his father’s failures to his siblings; he refers to him as “the old man” with barely concealed contempt; and when his father needs practical help he finds reasons to be unavailable. He tells himself this is justified because of the past. It may be understandable. But it is not honour. Paul’s command does not come with a clause for sufficient parental failure.
  • Boundary without dishonour: Sophie’s mother is controlling and regularly undermines Sophie’s parenting decisions in front of the children. Sophie has decided, after patient conversation that changed nothing, that her mother may not visit unsupervised for now. She tells her mother this calmly, without contempt, expressing love and the hope that things will change. She continues to call, to include her in family events on appropriate occasions, and to speak of her with respect to the children. This is honour with a boundary — neither doormat nor exile.

cf. Exod. 20:12; Mark 7:9–13; 1 Tim. 5:4, 8; Prov. 23:22; Col. 3:20.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prohibition is precise: do not parorgizete — exasperate, embitter, provoke. The word carries the weight of constant, demoralising criticism, unreasonable demands, or the cold withdrawal of love. These break the spirit rather than shape it.

The positive command is threefold in its depth: ektrephete (nourish, bring to full growth), paideia (structured training and correction), nouthesia (verbal instruction, counsel, admonition) — and all of it kyriou, of the Lord. The father is not forming the child in the father’s image but in the Lord’s image. The whole household is under Christ.

What provoking to anger looks like — and what to stop. Paul’s prohibition covers any pattern of fathering that consistently produces discouragement, bitterness, or the quiet conclusion in a child that they can never be enough. This is not about a bad day or a sharp word regretted and repaired; it is about patterns. The following are the most common forms:

  • Criticism without affirmation. The father who only notices what is wrong — the B instead of the A, the missed goal, the room not tidy enough — and rarely or never names what is right, slowly teaches the child that they are fundamentally inadequate. Children who grow up without ever hearing genuine, specific praise from their father carry that absence into adulthood. cf. Col. 3:21: “fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.”
  • Unrealistic or shifting expectations. The father whose standards are never quite met, who moves the goalposts, whose approval is permanently just out of reach — produces children who either drive themselves into the ground trying to earn what is never given, or give up entirely. Both are provocation.
  • Harshness and humiliation. Anger that shouts, demeans, or ridicules — especially in front of others — does not produce respect; it produces fear and, eventually, contempt. A father who humiliates his child for failing provokes the very resentment he may later be bewildered by.
  • Absence and emotional unavailability. The father who is physically present but emotionally absent — behind a screen, always busy, never genuinely interested in the child’s inner world — communicates that the child is not worth his full attention. This is a quiet form of provocation that leaves deep marks.
  • Inconsistency. Rigid punishment one day, indifference the next. Rules enforced when the father is in a bad mood and ignored when he is not. The child who cannot predict the father cannot trust him — and a child who cannot trust their father has no stable foundation for trusting anyone, including God.
  • Comparing to siblings or peers. “Why can’t you be more like your brother?” is one of the most reliably provoking sentences a father can speak. Comparison communicates that the child’s own identity is deficient, and it poisons the relationship between siblings at the same time.

What nurturing in the discipline and instruction of the Lord looks like — at different ages.

Young children (ages 2–7):

  • Be present and physically affectionate. A young child’s primary language is physical presence and touch. The father who gets on the floor, reads the story, plays the game, and is genuinely there — unhurried, undistracted — is doing some of his most important work. This is ektrephete: nourishing the soil before anything else is planted in it.
  • Establish clear, consistent, loving boundaries. Young children thrive on structure. Paideia at this age is primarily consistent, calm, consequence-based training: “we do not hit,” “we tell the truth,” followed by consistent and proportionate consequences when boundaries are crossed. The father who enforces the boundary with warmth and without rage is teaching the child that the world is ordered — and that the one who maintains order loves them.
  • Begin naming God in the ordinary. Before formal instruction, comes the habit of God-talk in daily life: “God made that butterfly;” “let’s thank God for our food;” “God sees when we are kind.” Deuteronomy 6:7 — “talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way.” The father who weaves God into ordinary conversation is doing more than he knows.
  • Pray with them by name, aloud, for specific things. The young child who hears their father pray for them by name — for their fears, their friendships, their day at school — receives one of the most formative experiences of childhood: their father taking them before God.

Older children and pre-teens (ages 8–12):

  • Show genuine interest in their world. Ask about their friendships, their interests, their fears — and listen to the answer. The father who knows the name of his child’s best friend, their favourite subject, and what they are currently anxious about, has the relational capital to speak into their life. The father who does not know these things has not yet bought the right to be heard on what matters.
  • Correct privately and specifically. Nouthesia at this age means naming what was wrong, explaining why, and pointing toward what right looks like — done privately, calmly, and connected to character rather than just behaviour. Not “you were rude” but “when you spoke to your mother that way, you were treating her as less than she deserves. That is not who I want you to be, and it is not who God made you to be.”
  • Introduce them to Scripture as alive, not as duty. Reading the Bible together at this age works best when the father brings genuine questions: “what do you think that means?” “does that surprise you?” “does that change anything for you this week?” The child who sees their father genuinely engaged with Scripture — not performing devotion but actually curious — catches something that cannot be taught directly.
  • Name their gifts and speak vision into them. A father who says “I see that God has given you a gift for encouraging people — that matters” or “the way you stuck with that when it was hard tells me something about your character” is speaking the nouthesia that forms identity. Children at this age are asking “who am I?” — the father’s answer is one of the most powerful they will receive.

Teenagers (ages 13–18):

  • Earn the right to speak by staying in the relationship. The teenager who has experienced their father as consistently present, genuinely interested, and safe to talk to will bring the hard questions to him. The father who has been largely absent and now wants to speak into the teenager’s faith and choices will find the door closed — not from rebellion but from a relational deficit that was built up over years. Stay in the relationship through the awkward years, even when they seem uninterested.
  • Move from authority to influence. The primary mode of paideia shifts as the child matures: less imposition, more conversation. The father of a fifteen-year-old who still parents primarily through command will lose them. The father who asks “what do you think?” and listens to the answer, who shares his own reasoning rather than just his conclusions, who admits uncertainty and models the pursuit of wisdom rather than the performance of it — is building something that will outlast the teenage years.
  • Address the hard questions honestly. The teenager is meeting the world — its sexuality, its scepticism, its suffering, its alternative gospels. Nouthesia at this age means engaging these questions with them rather than avoiding them. The father who says “that’s a great question — let’s think about it together” and who does not panic when the teenager doubts, models the faith he wants to pass on: honest, searching, and grounded.
  • Let them see your own walk with God. More is caught than taught. The teenager who sees their father pray privately, struggle honestly with Scripture, confess sin to God and to others, and return to Christ after failure, is receiving the most persuasive apologetic for the faith there is: a real person, living it, imperfectly but genuinely. cf. Deut. 6:6–9; Ps. 78:4–7; Prov. 4:1–4.

The goal throughout all ages is not a child who performs Christianity in front of their father, but a child who has tasted the goodness of God in their own heart because their father kept pointing them there. The father does not save his children — only God does that. But he is the primary human instrument through which God most often chooses to work. The responsibility is enormous. The grace available for it is more enormous still. cf. Deut. 6:4–9; Ps. 78:4–7; Prov. 22:6; Col. 3:21.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul addresses the slave first — itself a gesture of moral dignity in a world where slaves were often treated as property without standing. The command is for whole-hearted service: “fear and trembling” is not terror but the solemn awareness of standing before the living God. “With a sincere heart” (en haplotēti tēs kardias) — singleness of heart, without duplicity. “As you would Christ” — the real master is not the human employer but the Lord who observes all and to whom account is given. This fundamentally relativizes every human authority without removing the obligation of faithful service.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Eye-service” (ophthalmodoulia) — Paul coins a word: working only when watched, performing only for the observing eye. This is the default mode of coerced labor. The alternative is not better performance management but a different master: “bondservants of Christ.” When the ultimate audience is Christ — who sees all, records all, and will reward all — the human supervisor’s presence or absence becomes irrelevant. “From the heart” and “with a good will” — the quality of the work changes entirely when the audience changes. Labor offered to the Lord is worship; labor performed for human approval is performance.

What this looks like today. The slave-master relationship of Paul’s world has no direct equivalent, but the principle maps precisely onto the modern workplace — and onto every context where a Christian works under human authority.

Chloe is an account manager at a marketing firm. Her manager is demanding and not always fair; credit for her work has occasionally been taken by others, and she has been passed over for a promotion she deserved. The temptation is the one Paul names: eye-service. Do the minimum when the manager is not watching. Invest effort only in work that will be seen and recognised. Take the occasional shortcut on the project that no one will scrutinise. After all, why give full effort to a system that does not fully reward it?

Paul’s answer is not a better argument for harder work. It is a different audience. Chloe is not, in the deepest sense, working for her manager or for her company. She is working for Christ — who was present in the meeting where her credit was taken, who saw the extra hour she put in on the proposal no one noticed, who will miss nothing at the final accounting (v. 8). This changes everything — not her circumstances but her interior posture. The quality of her work is no longer hostage to the fairness of her employer. She works with a good will not because the system deserves it but because her Master does.

In practice this means:

  • The same quality of work whether or not the manager is in the building. The Christian employee who works differently when unobserved has two standards — one for human eyes and one for when they think no one is watching. Paul calls this ophthalmodoulia and refuses it. The one who is always watching is Christ, and his standard does not change with the supervisor’s schedule.
  • Integrity in the small things no one will ever check. The expense report filled in accurately when no one would notice the difference. The task completed properly when a corner could easily have been cut. The honest answer given when a vague one would have been safe. These are the daily practice of working “as to the Lord.”
  • A good will toward difficult colleagues and managers. “With a good will” (met’ eunoias) means genuine goodwill — not performed collegiality while harbouring resentment, but the actual disposition to want the best for the person above you, even when that person is hard to work for. This is not naive; it is costly. But it flows from the same logic: this manager is not my ultimate employer, and my attitude toward them is itself an act of worship or its absence.
  • Releasing the outcome of fairness to God. Verse 8 gives the ground for all of this: “whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord.” The Christian who has been overlooked, undervalued, or treated unjustly at work is not owed nothing. They are owed everything — by a Master who does not forget, who keeps perfect accounts, and who will settle them fully. This is not passive resignation; it is the freedom to work wholeheartedly without needing the human system to be fair first.

The result, when this is genuinely lived, is a Christian worker who stands out not because they are performing Christian witness as a strategy, but because something in the quality of their work and the character of their presence is different. People notice a person who does not change when the boss leaves the room. That consistency is itself a testimony. cf. Col. 3:23–24; 1 Pet. 2:18–19; Matt. 6:4.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary: The great equalizer: divine justice makes no distinction of social status. “Whether he is a bondservant or is free” — the slave and the freeman stand before the same judge and receive the same reward for faithful labor. No deed done for the Lord is wasted, overlooked, or unrewarded, whether it was performed in a position of prestige or in a slave quarter. Calvin: “God is no respecter of persons; the service of the most humbled slave, done in faith, is as acceptable to him as the offering of kings.” This is a profound subversion of every social hierarchy: the eternal calculus does not follow the ledgers of Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master is brought under the same rubric as the slave. He has a Master. His authority is delegated and conditional. He is to treat his slaves with the same integrity of heart he expects from them — “do the same.” The specific prohibition — stop threatening — targets the master’s most characteristic abuse of power. The reason is theological: God shows no partiality. Social status confers no advantage before the throne of heaven.

This was not an anti-slavery manifesto in the modern sense; it was something more radical in the long run — it placed master and slave under the same moral governance, the same eternal accountability, the same Lord. The logic, followed to its conclusion, is incompatible with slavery as an institution.

What this means in today’s corporate world. The master-slave dynamic of Paul’s world has no direct modern equivalent, but the power differential between employer and employee — manager and team, director and staff, owner and contractor — maps closely enough that Paul’s logic lands with full force. The Christian who holds authority over others in the workplace stands exactly where the master stood: with delegated power, under the same ultimate Master, and without partiality before his throne.

“Do the same to them” — the reciprocity is striking. Paul has just told employees to work with whole-hearted integrity, as to the Lord. Now he turns to the employer and says: the same standard applies to you. You do not get a different set of rules because you hold the power. In practice this means:

  • Treat people as persons, not as resources. The language of modern business — human resources, headcount, bandwidth, capacity — reduces persons to units of productivity. The Christian manager resists this at the level of actual behaviour: knowing the names and situations of the people who report to them, caring whether a team member is struggling at home, noticing when someone is carrying more than is visible in the performance metrics. People are made in the image of God. The way they are managed is either consistent with that dignity or it is not.
  • Give credit where it is due. One of the most common forms of workplace injustice is the manager who takes credit for the work of those below them or who fails to advocate for their team’s recognition. Paul’s “do the same” means: if you expect your employees to work as though the Lord sees them, work as though the Lord sees you — including in the room where credit is assigned.
  • Pay fairly and promptly. The Old Testament is sharp on this: Leviticus 19:13 — “the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning;” James 5:4 — “the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you.” The Christian business owner or finance director who delays payment to suppliers or employees for cash-flow advantage, or who structures compensation to extract maximum work for minimum cost, is answerable to the same Master as the employee who cuts corners when no one is watching.
  • Create conditions in which people can do good work. The manager who sets unrealistic deadlines, who withholds the information a team needs to succeed, who provides no feedback and then penalises poor performance — is provoking the workplace equivalent of what Paul forbids fathers from doing to children (v. 4). The Christian employer invests in the development of those under them, communicates clearly, and builds structures that allow people to flourish rather than merely survive.

“Stop threatening” — Paul’s specific prohibition targets the most characteristic abuse of managerial power: using the threat of job loss, poor review, demotion, or public humiliation to extract compliance. In today’s corporate world this takes recognisable forms:

  • The manager who rules by fear — whose team is productive because they are afraid, not because they are motivated.
  • The leader who uses performance reviews as a weapon rather than a development tool.
  • The executive who makes examples of people publicly in order to keep others compliant.
  • The employer who reminds employees — subtly or otherwise — how easily they could be replaced.

Paul names this and prohibits it. Not because it is commercially unwise (though it often is), but because it treats persons as means rather than ends, exploits the power differential God has granted as a stewardship, and does precisely what the master’s own Master never does to him.

“He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him.” This is the levelling phrase that changes everything. In the boardroom, the CEO holds enormous power over those below. Before the throne of God, they stand on exactly the same ground as the intern. Title, salary, equity stake, corner office — none of it buys a single degree of advantage in that courtroom. The Christian executive who genuinely believes this will manage differently: not from a platform of permanent superiority but from the sober awareness that they are stewards of delegated authority, answerable for how they have used it.

A concrete picture: Richard is CEO of a mid-sized company. His company is under financial pressure and restructuring is on the table. The advisors recommend announcing redundancies with minimal notice to prevent flight risk. Richard decides instead to be transparent with the team about the situation, to give as much notice as legally and financially possible, to write personal references for every person made redundant, and to ensure the severance process is handled with dignity rather than efficiency. It costs more and it is harder. But Richard has a Master who saw every person on that list before they were born and knows their name. Managing “as to the Lord” means that even the hardest business decisions are made with that awareness in the room. cf. Lev. 19:13; James 5:4; Col. 4:1; Prov. 22:16; Luke 16:10.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter's great climax — and it arrives without warning, like a general stepping out of his tent to address his troops before the decisive battle. "Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might." Everything that has preceded — the cosmic vision of God's purposes, the theology of grace, the ethics of the Spirit-filled community, the transformed household — now finds its context: the Christian life is warfare. Not metaphorical warfare, not a polite spiritual competition, but genuine, cosmic, personal, urgent conflict with "the rulers, the authorities, the cosmic powers over this present darkness, the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" (v.12).

The armour Paul describes is not human equipment; it is divine provision. Each piece is identified with a theological reality rather than a military material. The belt is truth. The breastplate is righteousness. The boots are readiness given by the gospel of peace. The shield is faith. The helmet is salvation. The sword is the word of God. Roman soldiers would have recognized every item in this list; Paul is taking the most powerful military image of his world and filling it entirely with theological content, because the battle that matters is not on the human plane and cannot be won with human weapons.

The repeated command is to stand — four times in seven verses (vv.11, 13, 14). Not to advance on our own initiative, not to conquer by our own strength, but to hold the ground that Christ has already secured against a defeated enemy who refuses to concede. The Christian stands in the victory of the resurrection, armed with the provisions of the ascended Lord, and sustained — above all things — by prayer. "Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication" (v.18) — the armour is not self-sustaining; it functions within an ongoing relationship with the Commander, through whose power alone the standing is possible.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Warfare and the Victory of Christ

The passage grounds the doctrine of spiritual warfare in the victory already achieved by Christ. The Reformers consistently insisted that the Christian fights from victory, not toward it. At the cross and resurrection, Christ decisively defeated the powers: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). The "rulers and authorities" of Ephesians 6:12 are already defeated enemies — real, malevolent, and active, but operating under the authority of One who has conquered them. The Christian's warfare is not the decisive battle; it is the mopping-up operation conducted in light of a victory already won.

This context — victory already achieved — is what makes "standing" the characteristic posture of the Christian warrior rather than "advancing." Paul does not say "take more territory." He says "stand." Hold what Christ has secured. Don't give ground to a defeated enemy. Don't abandon the position that grace has placed you in. This is not a passive posture; it requires every piece of armour, every act of faith, every prayer offered in the Spirit. But it is a posture of confidence, not of uncertainty — the confidence of those who know how the battle ends and who are fighting in the strength of its Victor.

Prayer (vv.18–20) is the atmosphere in which the armoured Christian stands. It is "at all times in the Spirit" — not occasional, not formal, but the constant, Spirit-sustained reaching toward the Commander. Paul's request for prayer for himself (vv.19–20) is among the most searching things in the letter. The apostle who has written the most magnificent theological letter in the New Testament asks his readers to pray that he would have the boldness to speak the gospel clearly. He is acutely aware that the proclamation of the gospel is itself a spiritual warfare activity, requiring not merely intellectual preparation but Spirit-given courage and divine enablement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city saturated with occult practice. The book of Acts records that when the gospel came to Ephesus, it confronted demonic powers directly — the sons of Sceva, the burning of the magic books, the riot engineered by Demetrius the silversmith whose trade in Artemis-shrines was threatened (Acts 19). The Ephesian Christians knew, from personal experience, that spiritual warfare was real. When Paul tells them to stand against "the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places," he is not speaking metaphorically to a congregation that has only ever faced theoretical opposition. He is arming people who have already been in the fight.

Now: The tendency in contemporary Christianity is to spiritualise spiritual warfare into invisibility (it's just a metaphor for human sin and social structures) or to sensationalise it into obsession (seeing demonic activity behind every difficulty). Paul's teaching steers between both errors. The powers are real — personal, intelligent, malevolent. But they are defeated — operating under the authority of the risen Christ who has already triumphed over them. The Christian response is neither to ignore them nor to be paralyzed by them, but to stand — in the truth, in righteousness, in the gospel, in faith, in salvation, in the word of God, and in unceasing prayer. This is neither the naivety of the denier nor the anxiety of the obsessed. It is the steady, armoured confidence of those who know their Commander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Finally” marks the climactic practical section of the letter. The exhortation to strength is passive: endunamousthe — be empowered, receive strength from without. The source is “the Lord” — the exalted Christ who has already defeated every enemy (1:20–22). “The strength of his might” (kratous tēs ischyos autou) — three terms for power, the same language used in 1:19 for the power that raised Christ from the dead. The battle Paul is about to describe is not fought in the believer’s own resources but in the inexhaustible power of the one who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.
